title: How animals send messages: smell, colour, sound, touch and echoes

summary.text: A female silk moth sits still on a leaf and makes no sound. Yet a male moth finds her in the dark. She gives off a smell called a pheromone, and his feathery antennae catch it. Animals, including humans, send messages in four ways: by smell, by sight, by sound and by touch. Your child tests how long a smell message lasts after the sender has left the room. They also find a steel plate with their eyes covered, using only echoes, as bats and dolphins do.
summary.art: A pale silk moth sitting on a mulberry leaf at night, and a second moth with wide feathery antennae flying towards her through the dark.

intro.hook: A tigress sprays a tree and walks away. Three days later, another tiger sniffs the tree and learns that she lives here. How did a message pass between two animals who never met?
intro.text: The tigress left a smell on the bark, and the smell stayed after she had gone. A smell is one way to send a message. A peacock uses colour. A frog uses a call. A monkey uses her fingers. Each way works well in some places and badly in others. In this unit you leave smell marks on paper and test how long they last. You also cover your eyes and find a steel plate by listening for echoes, as a bat finds a moth.
intro.art: A tigress walking away from a tree in a dry forest, with a wet mark on the bark, and a second tiger far behind on the same path.

outcomes: I can name the four channels of animal signals and give an example of each.
I can explain what a pheromone is, and why a smell mark still works after the sender has gone.
I can test fairly how long a smell mark lasts, and say what my results show.
I can explain how colours, displays and dances send messages, and why they need light and a clear view.
I can explain what calls and songs do well, and name sounds too high or too low for humans.
I can explain how touch and vibration carry messages, such as grooming and the shaking of a spider's web.
I can explain how bats and dolphins find things by echolocation, and test whether I can hear an echo myself.
I can choose the best channel for a dark, noisy or distant place, and say how signals are overheard.

terms.meaning: Something one animal does or makes that carries a message to another animal.
terms.example: A dog's growl is a signal. So is a peacock's raised train.
terms.art: A dog growling at a second dog, with a small arrow going from one to the other.

terms.meaning: The sender is the animal who gives the signal. The receiver is the animal who picks it up.
terms.example: When a frog calls, he is the sender. The female frog who hears him is the receiver.
terms.art: A male frog calling on a leaf, and a female frog on another leaf turning towards him.

terms.meaning: The way a signal travels from sender to receiver. The four main channels are smell, sight, sound and touch.
terms.example: A call travels on the sound channel. A scent mark travels on the smell channel.
terms.art: Four small pictures in a row: a nose, an eye, an ear and a hand.

terms.meaning: A chemical that an animal gives off, which changes what other animals of the same kind do.
terms.example: A female silk moth gives off a pheromone, and male silk moths walk towards it.
terms.art: A moth on a leaf with faint dotted lines drifting away from her body on the wind.

terms.meaning: A smell that an animal leaves on a tree, a wall or the ground for others to find later.
terms.example: A dog who wets a lamp post is leaving a scent mark.
terms.art: A street dog sniffing the bottom of a lamp post.

terms.meaning: A signal made for the eyes, using colour, shape or movement.
terms.example: A peacock spreading his train in front of a peahen is giving a display.
terms.art: A peacock with his train spread wide, and a brown peahen watching.

terms.meaning: Bright colours, such as orange with black, that tell hunters an animal tastes bad or can sting.
terms.example: The plain tiger butterfly is orange and black, and birds learn not to eat them.
terms.art: An orange and black butterfly on a milkweed flower, with a bird turning away.

terms.meaning: Sound that is too high for human ears to hear.
terms.example: Most bats call in ultrasound, so a bat flying past you seems silent.
terms.art: A bat with sound rings coming from the mouth, and a child below hearing nothing.

terms.meaning: Sound that is too low for human ears to hear.
terms.example: Elephants make deep rumbles, and part of each rumble is infrasound.
terms.art: Two elephants far apart on a plain, joined by long, widely spaced sound rings.

terms.meaning: A fast shaking back and forth. Animals can feel vibrations through a web, a leaf or the ground.
terms.example: A spider feels the vibration when a fly lands on her web.
terms.art: A spider at the middle of a web with small wavy lines along one thread.

terms.meaning: A sound that bounces off something and comes back to you.
terms.example: Shout in an empty hall, and you hear your shout come back as an echo.
terms.art: A child shouting towards a big wall, with curved lines going out and coming back.

terms.meaning: Finding where things are by making a sound and listening to its echoes.
terms.example: A bat calls, and the echo from a moth tells her where the moth is.
terms.art: A bat sending sound rings towards a moth, and smaller rings coming back to the bat's ears.

terms.meaning: Picking up a signal that was meant for someone else.
terms.example: A hunting bat hears a frog calling for a mate and flies towards the call.
terms.art: A small frog calling on a leaf at night while a bat swoops towards him from behind.

explanations.definition: A signal is something one animal does or makes that carries a message to another animal. A channel is the way the signal travels: smell, sight, sound or touch.
explanations.description: Every signal needs a sender and a receiver. The sender must make the signal, and the receiver must have a body that can pick it up. A smell needs a nose or an antenna. A colour needs an eye. A call needs an ear. A touch needs skin or hairs that feel. Most animals use more than one channel. A street dog growls, shows her teeth, raises the hair on her back and leaves scent marks. Humans are animals too, and we use all four channels. We speak, we smile, we hug, and our noses can tell family from strangers. This unit takes the channels one at a time, and then compares them.
examples: Smell: an ant leaves a scent trail to food.
Sight: a fan-throated lizard flashes a blue, black and orange throat.
Sound: a koel calls from a mango tree before the rains.
Touch: a bonnet macaque picks through her friend's fur.
explanations.art: A square cut into four parts, each showing one channel: an ant trail, a lizard with a bright throat fan, a calling koel and two macaques grooming.

explanations.concept: Pheromones are messages made of smell
explanations.definition: A pheromone is a chemical that an animal gives off, which changes what other animals of the same kind do.
explanations.description: A pheromone is made of molecules, which are tiny particles far too small to see. The molecules leave the sender's body and drift on the air or stay on a surface. When they reach the antenna or nose of the right animal, that animal acts. A female silk moth gives off a pheromone called bombykol, and a male walks upwind until he finds her. A honeybee who stings gives off an alarm pheromone that smells like bananas, and other bees rush to the spot. Ants know their nestmates by the smell on their bodies. Some pheromones are made of small, light molecules. These spread fast and fade within minutes, which suits an alarm. Others are heavy and oily. These stay on a tree for days, which suits a mark that says who lives here. A smell also goes round corners and works in the dark. Its weak point is speed. A smell is slow to spread, and the sender cannot take it back or change it quickly.
examples: A tigress sprays a tree, and other tigers can read the mark for days.
An ant who finds a dead beetle lays a scent trail, and her sisters follow it.
A house cat rubs her cheek on a chair leg and leaves her own smell there.
explanations.art: A cat rubbing her cheek against a chair leg, with a faint patch drawn on the wood where she rubbed.

explanations.concept: Colours and displays are messages for the eyes
explanations.definition: A display is a signal made for the eyes. It uses colour, shape or movement.
explanations.description: Light travels very fast and in straight lines. So a display reaches the receiver at once, and the receiver sees exactly where the sender is. A male fan-throated lizard in Maharashtra stands on a stone and flicks out a bright throat fan. A male fiddler crab on a Kerala mudflat waves one huge claw. Both displays are big, bright and repeated, because a small or dull signal is missed from far away. Some colours are warnings. The plain tiger butterfly is orange and black, and tastes bad to birds. A bird who tries one remembers the colours. A display has two weak points. It needs light, and it needs a clear view. A leaf, a wall or the night can block it. A hunter can see it too, so a bright animal is easier to catch. Many animals show their colours only when they need to. The lizard folds his fan away, and the peacock lowers his train.
examples: A peacock raises his train and shakes it in front of a peahen.
A plain tiger butterfly's orange and black wings warn birds not to eat them.
A street dog tucks her tail and lowers her body to show she does not want a fight.
explanations.art: A male fan-throated lizard standing on a stone with a bright blue, black and orange throat fan pushed out.

explanations.concept: A dance is a message made of movement
explanations.definition: A dance is a display in which the order and the timing of the movements carry the message.
explanations.description: A pair of sarus cranes in a wet field bow, leap and call together. The dance tells each crane that the other is healthy and ready to nest. A male jumping spider lifts his front legs and steps from side to side in front of a female. If his steps are wrong, she may treat him as food. A honeybee dances on the comb in the dark hive. The bees who follow her learn where the flowers are. You will learn to read the bee dance in a later unit. Small frogs called dancing frogs live beside loud streams in the Western Ghats. A male calls, and he also stretches out a back leg and spreads his white foot. Scientists think the foot wave helps because the stream is so loud that a call alone is often lost. A dance costs energy and time, so a dancer shows that they are strong enough to pay for it.
examples: Sarus cranes in Uttar Pradesh leap and bow to each other.
A male jumping spider on a wall waves his front legs at a female.
A dancing frog in Karnataka waves a white foot beside a noisy stream.
explanations.art: A small brown frog on a wet rock beside a rushing stream, with one back leg stretched out and the white webbed foot spread wide.

explanations.concept: Calls and songs, and the sounds humans cannot hear
explanations.definition: A call or a song is a signal made of sound. Sound spreads in every direction, passes round trees and works in the dark.
explanations.description: A sound is fast, and the sender can change it or stop it in a moment. That makes sound good for alarms and for calling over long distances. Its weak point is that a sound is gone as soon as it ends, and anyone nearby can hear it. Human ears hear only a part of all sound. Sound too high for us is called ultrasound. Bats, mice and many moths use it. Sound too low for us is called infrasound. Elephants make deep rumbles that can reach other elephants several kilometres away. Male humpback whales sing songs that last many minutes, and whales far away can hear them. Water carries sound more than four times as fast as air does. Each bottlenose dolphin has their own whistle, called a signature whistle. Other dolphins copy that whistle to call them, a little as we use a name.
examples: A male cricket rubs his wings together, and females walk towards the sound.
Frogs in a paddy field call after the first monsoon rain, and each kind has a different call.
An elephant mother rumbles, and her family far across the forest turns towards her.
explanations.art: A line showing sound from low to high, with an elephant at the low end, a child in the middle and a bat at the high end.

explanations.definition: A touch signal passes when two animals are in contact. A vibration signal passes through something they both touch, such as a web, a stem or the ground.
explanations.description: Touch is the most private channel, because only the animal who is touched receives it. Bonnet macaques sit and pick through each other's fur. This is called grooming. Grooming removes dirt and insects, and it also keeps friendships strong. Elephants greet by touching trunks to each other's mouths. A honeybee asks a sister for food by tapping her with her antennae. Vibration lets a touch travel a little further. A spider rests at the middle of her web with her feet on the threads. A struggling fly shakes the web one way, and the wind shakes it another way. A male spider who comes to visit plucks the threads in his own rhythm. That way she does not mistake him for food. Elephants also feel deep rumbles through the ground with their feet and trunks. The weak point of touch is distance. The sender has to be close.
examples: Two langurs sit on a temple wall, and one grooms the other's back.
A mother dog licks her newborn pups.
A spider runs along the exact thread that a trapped fly is shaking.
explanations.art: Two bonnet macaques on a wall, one parting the fur on the other's shoulder with her fingers.

explanations.definition: Echolocation means making a sound and using its echoes to find where things are.
explanations.description: An echo is a sound that has bounced off something and come back. A hunting bat makes very short, very loud calls in ultrasound. Each call bounces off a moth, a leaf or a wall. The echo from a near thing comes back sooner than the echo from a far thing. So the time between call and echo tells the bat the distance. Bats are not blind. They echolocate because eyes are little use for catching a small insect in the dark. Large fruit bats, such as the Indian flying fox, do not echolocate. They find fruit with their eyes and noses. Dolphins echolocate with clicks. A dolphin makes the clicks inside her nose passages, and a pad of fat in her forehead aims them forward. The echoes return through her lower jaw to her ears. The Ganges river dolphin is almost blind and lives in muddy water, so she finds fish almost entirely by echoes. Echolocation is not a message to another animal. The same animal is the sender and the receiver. Yet others can overhear it.
examples: A small bat circles a street lamp and catches insects that she cannot see.
A Ganges river dolphin in the muddy water near Bhagalpur finds a fish by clicking.
Some blind people click their tongues and hear where walls and doors are.
explanations.art: A bat in flight with sound rings going out towards a moth, and fainter rings coming back to the bat's large ears.

explanations.concept: Every channel has gains and costs
explanations.definition: No channel is the best everywhere. Each one works well in some conditions and badly in others.
explanations.description: Compare the four. A smell lasts after the sender leaves and goes round corners, but it is slow and cannot be changed quickly. A display is instant and shows exactly where the sender is, but it needs light and a clear view. A sound is fast, works in the dark and goes round trees. But it ends at once, and everyone nearby hears it. A touch is private and hard to mistake, but the sender must be close. So the place decides the channel. Moths fly at night in forests, and they use smell. Lizards live on open ground in bright sun, and they use colour. Frogs call at night, when colours are hard to see. Animals who live in a difficult place often use two channels together. The dancing frog beside a loud stream does this.
examples: Night in a thick forest: smell and sound work, but a display does not.
Open ground at noon: a display works well.
Muddy river water: sound works, and sight does not.
explanations.art: A table with four rows for smell, sight, sound and touch, and ticks and crosses under the headings Works in the dark, Goes round corners, Lasts after the sender leaves and Fast.

explanations.concept: A signal can be overheard, and a signal can be false
explanations.definition: Eavesdropping means picking up a signal that was meant for someone else. A false signal is one that leads the receiver to do something that helps the sender and harms the receiver.
explanations.description: A signal goes out into the world, and the sender has no control over who receives it. In Central America a male túngara frog calls to females. A hunting bat hears the same call and flies to him. Many tiger moths have ears that hear bat calls. When a bat comes near, such a moth dives away, and some kinds click back and spoil the bat's echoes. Signals can also be false. A koel lays her egg in a crow's nest. The koel chick begs so well that the crows feed them. In the Kalahari Desert, fork-tailed drongos give alarm calls when no danger is near. Then they take the food that frightened meerkats drop. False signals cannot become too common. If most alarm calls were false, the receivers would stop responding to them.
examples: A bat hears a calling frog and hunts him.
A tiger moth hears a bat and drops out of the way.
A koel chick in a crow's nest begs, and the crows feed them.
explanations.art: A tiger moth with folded wings dropping towards the ground while a bat passes just above.

explanations.concept: Does a signal tell, or does it push?
explanations.definition: Scientists agree that signals change what receivers do. They disagree about the best way to describe what a signal is.
explanations.description: When a monkey gives an alarm call and the others climb, what has passed between them? There are two main ways to describe it, and both are used by working scientists.
examples: A vervet monkey gives a 'leopard' call and the others climb trees.
A male frog's deep call draws a female towards him.

perspectives.who: Scientists who speak of information, such as Dorothy Cheney and Robert Seyfarth
perspectives.explanation: A signal carries information. The alarm call tells the listeners that a leopard is near. They use what they have learned to choose what to do.

perspectives.who: Scientists who speak of influence, such as Richard Dawkins and John Krebs in 1978
perspectives.explanation: A signal is a way for the sender to change the receiver's behaviour. On this view we should ask what the signal makes the receiver do, and whom that helps.
Both are true. Animals think, feel and choose. A sender signals for their own reasons, and a receiver weighs the signal and decides. Most signals last only because both sides gain from them.

explanations.art: Two thought bubbles over a calling monkey: one shows a leopard, and the other shows monkeys climbing a tree.

agreed.text: Animals signal by smell, sight, sound and touch, and many use several channels at once.
agreed.evidence: Scientists have watched and recorded signals in thousands of kinds of animals, from ants to whales.

agreed.text: Pheromones are real chemicals, and each has a particular make-up.
agreed.evidence: In 1959 Adolf Butenandt's team purified the silk moth pheromone bombykol. A tiny amount of this one chemical made male moths flutter their wings.

agreed.text: Bats and toothed whales such as dolphins find things by echolocation.
agreed.evidence: From 1938 Donald Griffin used a detector that picks up ultrasound, and found that flying bats call all the time. He and Robert Galambos then tested bats among wires. Bats with their ears or mouths covered crashed. Bats with their eyes covered did not.

agreed.text: Many animals use sounds that humans cannot hear.
agreed.evidence: Special microphones for very high and very low sounds record bat calls, mouse songs and elephant rumbles.

agreed.text: A signal can be overheard by animals it was not meant for.
agreed.evidence: Michael Ryan and Merlin Tuttle showed that fringe-lipped bats fly to loudspeakers playing túngara frog calls.

agreed.text: The place where an animal lives shapes the signals they use.
agreed.evidence: Dancing frogs beside loud streams add a foot wave to their call. Animals of the night and of muddy water depend on smell and sound.

challenging.who: A common saying: 'as blind as a bat'.
challenging.for: Bats fly at night and many have small eyes.
challenging.against: All bats have working eyes. Large fruit bats find food mainly by sight and smell. Small bats echolocate as well as see.

challenging.claim: A peahen chooses the peacock with the most eyespots on his train.
challenging.who: Marion Petrie and her team in England, in 1991.
challenging.for: In their studies, males with more eyespots won more mates, and males with some eyespots cut off did worse.
challenging.against: A seven-year study in Japan by Mariko Takahashi's team, published in 2008, found no such choice. The train matters, but what peahens look for is still argued.

challenging.claim: Humans have pheromones that change how other people behave.
challenging.who: Many perfume advertisements, and some early studies.
challenging.for: Humans have many scent glands, and babies can find their mother by smell.
challenging.against: No human pheromone has yet been purified and shown to work in careful tests. The zoologist Tristram Wyatt reviewed the evidence in 2015 and found none that held up.

challenging.claim: Animal signals are only outbursts of feeling and say nothing about the world.
challenging.for: A scream of fear and a purr of comfort do come with strong feelings.
challenging.against: Vervet monkeys give different alarm calls for leopards, eagles and snakes, and listeners respond to each in the right way. A honeybee's dance tells her sisters where food is.

challenging.claim: Plants send and receive signals too.
challenging.who: Plant scientists such as Richard Karban.
challenging.for: Sagebrush plants that are cut give off chemicals, and neighbours that sense them are eaten less by insects. Plants signal, sense and respond.
challenging.against: Some scientists say the neighbour is only picking up a leak. They keep the word 'signal' for messages that evolved to be sent.

big_questions.q: A tigress marks a tree and no other tiger ever passes by. Was the mark a message?
big_questions.hint: Think about a letter that is written but never opened.

big_questions.q: A bat's call is overheard by a moth, who escapes. Did the bat send the moth a message?
big_questions.hint: The bat did not gain from it. Does a message need the sender to want it received?

big_questions.q: Elephants and bats use sounds we cannot hear. What else might be passing around us, unnoticed?
big_questions.hint: People found these signals only after building new instruments.

big_questions.q: If you could add one new sense to your body, which signals would you want to pick up?
big_questions.hint: Think about what a dog learns at a lamp post, or a bat on a dark night.

big_questions.q: Writing lets a human message last after the sender has left. Is writing a kind of scent mark?
big_questions.hint: Compare what you found in the Smell Mark Test with a note left on the fridge.

big_questions.q: People have beamed radio messages into space. If someone is out there, would their bodies be able to receive them?
big_questions.hint: A signal needs a receiver whose senses fit it. A moth's pheromone means nothing to a crow.

story.title: The White Foot at the Stream
story.note: Nethra, Sudha Chikkamma and their frog count are made up. These facts are real: dancing frogs live beside fast streams in the Western Ghats, they are active by day, the males call and also stretch out a back leg and spread a white foot, and one kind is named after Kottigehara in Karnataka. Scientists who studied these frogs found that the foot wave goes together with the call beside noisy water.
text: Nethra had come to the hills near Kottigehara to count frogs with her aunt. So far she had counted none.

Her aunt, Sudha Chikkamma, studied frogs for a college in Mysuru. Every year, when the big rains ended, she came to this stream with a notebook, a torch and a tin of ragi biscuits. This year she had brought Nethra, who was nine, and who had promised not to complain about leeches.
The stream was loud. It came down over black rocks, white and fast, and its noise filled the whole valley. To say anything, they had to put their mouths close to each other's ears.

"They are here," Chikkamma shouted. "Each one is as small as your thumb and as brown as the rock. The males call, tick-tick-tick, like a tiny clock being wound. A call tells the females where he is. It tells other males that his rock is taken."
Nethra listened. She heard the stream, and nothing else.

"I am going across to look upstream," Chikkamma shouted. "Sit on this flat rock and watch. If you find one, call me." She walked over a fallen tree to the far bank, and soon she was twenty steps away, bent over her notebook.
Nethra sat. Sunlight came down through the leaves in small round patches. She stared at the wet rocks until her eyes ached. Leaf. Rock. Rock. Moss.
Then one piece of rock blinked.

He was sitting right at the edge of the water, no bigger than the top of her thumb. As she watched, the skin under his chin swelled into a small white bubble, and sank, and swelled again. He was calling. She could see him calling. She could not hear one tick of it.
She stood up carefully. "Chikkamma!" she shouted. Her aunt did not turn.
"CHIKKAMMA!" The stream took her voice the way it had taken the frog's. Twenty steps away, her aunt turned a page.

Nethra thought of throwing a pebble, but a pebble might frighten him. She thought of running across the fallen tree, but then she would lose the spot. Her hand went to the white cotton towel round her neck. She pulled it off, held it high in both hands, and swept it slowly from side to side.
Chikkamma's head came up at once. She waved, shut her notebook, and started back across the tree.
Nethra lowered the towel and looked for the frog. He was still there. And now he did something she had never seen a frog do.

He lifted one back leg. He stretched it out behind him, straight as a twig. Then he opened his toes. The skin between them was white, as white as her towel. He held the foot there, a small bright fan against the dark rock, and folded it away. Then he did it again.
On a rock on the other side of the water, something white opened and closed. A second frog had answered.
Chikkamma dropped down beside her, breathing hard. Nethra pointed at the frog. Then she pointed at her towel. Then she pointed at the white foot, which was opening again.
Her aunt laughed. Nethra could see the laugh but not hear it. Chikkamma put her mouth to Nethra's ear. "Yes," she shouted. "The very same reason."

That evening they sat on the verandah of the forest guard's house, where it was quiet enough to talk. "He does call," Chikkamma said. "A female very near him can hear it. But beside that water, most of a call is lost. So he sends the message a second way. A stream cannot drown a white foot."
"Why white?" asked Nethra.
"What colour was your towel? Would I have looked up for a brown one?"
Nethra thought about it. "But at night nobody could see his foot."
"That is right. A wave needs light. These frogs are busy in the daytime, so a wave works for them. Most frogs call at night, and they never wave at all."
Nethra opened her own notebook. Under the date she wrote: Frogs seen, 2. Messages seen, 3.
"Three?" said Chikkamma, reading over her shoulder.
"Two feet," said Nethra, "and one towel."

The next morning she went back to the flat rock alone and sat very still. After a while the frog lifted his leg and spread his white foot. Nethra kept her towel in her lap. She did not know yet what a wave from her would say to him.
story.epiphany: The stream drowned Nethra's shout, so she waved a white towel. Then she saw the frog do the same thing with his foot. When one channel is blocked, a signal has to travel on another.
ask: Why did the wave reach across the stream when the shout did not?
Why does a white foot work better than a brown one on a dark rock?
Where in your home would a wave fail and a call work?
