items.f: Two elephants meet. Each puts the tip of her trunk to the other's mouth.
items.b: Touch. This is a greeting between elephants who know each other.

items.f: A female silk moth sits still on a leaf with the tip of her body raised.
items.b: Smell. She is giving off a pheromone that draws males.

items.f: A street dog lowers her chest to the ground and wags her raised tail.
items.b: Sight. This bow invites another dog to play.

items.f: Frogs in a paddy field call loudly on the first night of rain.
items.b: Sound. Each kind of frog has a different call, so females find the right males.

items.f: A dancing frog beside a loud stream calls and also spreads a white foot.
items.b: Sound and sight. He uses two channels, so either token scores.

printables.title: 4 channel tokens: Smell, Sight, Sound, Touch. Print one set for each player

rules: One player is the reader. The reader takes the top card and reads the front aloud. The reader keeps the back hidden.
Every other player puts one channel token face down. Then everyone turns the tokens over together.
The reader reads the back. Every player whose token matches the channel on the back scores 1 point.
A player who also says what the message might be scores 1 more point. The reader decides, using the back of the card.
With two players, swap the reader's role after every card. The reader does not guess on their own card.
Playing alone? Read a card, say the channel aloud, then turn the card over. Score 1 point for each right channel.
After all 20 cards, the player with the most points wins. If you play alone, your score out of 20 is your result.

flow.do: Cut out the 20 cards and the tokens. Shuffle the cards into a pile. Give each player one set of four tokens.
flow.say: Each card describes a real signal that an animal gives. Your four tokens are the four channels: smell, sight, sound and touch. We will say which channel each signal uses.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards. Take four tokens.
flow.context: This is the first step of Which Channel. You set up the cards and the tokens.

flow.do: Play the first ten cards. After each card, read the back aloud. Ask the question below after card five.
flow.say: The reader reads the front. Choose a token and put it face down. Now turn it over. The reader reads the back. Who scored?
flow.kid: Listen to the card. Pick a channel token. Turn it over. Check the back.

ask.q: How did you decide which channel the signal uses?
good: I asked which body part would pick it up.
A nose picks up a smell, and an eye picks up a colour.
I thought about whether it would work in the dark.

flow.parent: A useful question for a stuck child is: which part of the receiver's body picks this up? One child can play alone or with you. With three or four players, take turns as the reader.
flow.context: In this step of Which Channel you play the first ten signal cards.

flow.do: Play the last ten cards the same way. Keep the score on a piece of paper.
flow.say: Ten more cards. This time, also try to say what the message is. A good guess at the message earns one more point.
flow.kid: Play ten more cards. Say what each message might be.
flow.context: In this step of Which Channel you play the last ten cards and guess each message.

flow.do: Count the points. Then sort all 20 cards into four piles by channel and look at the piles.
flow.say: Let us sort the cards into four piles, one for each channel. Which signals would still work at night? Which would work if the receiver came by a day later?
flow.kid: Sort the cards into four piles. Which signals work in the dark?

check.q: Which channel works in the dark and also lasts after the sender has gone?
check.why: A scent mark needs no light and stays on the tree. A display needs light. A sound works in the dark, but it ends when the sender stops.

flow.context: This is the last step of Which Channel. You sort the signal cards by channel and compare the piles.

games.title: Nestmate or Stranger? The smell pairs game
games.context: This is a memory game played with your nose. Ants know their own nestmates by smell, and here you find pairs of packets that smell the same.

setup.art: A grown-up at a kitchen counter folding small paper packets, with little heaps of cloves, cumin seeds, coffee powder and cardamom beside them.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up makes eight paper packets. Two packets hold each of the four smells.

setup.art: Eight folded paper packets in two rows of four on a table, each with a letter label from A to H.
setup.caption: 2. Stick a letter on each packet. Lay them in two rows of four.

setup.art: A child holding one packet under her nose with her eyes closed, and a second packet in the other hand.
setup.caption: 3. Sniff two packets. Say 'nestmates' if they smell the same.

printables.title: Score sheet: 4 pairs to find
items: Pair 1: packet ___ and packet ___. Found by ___
Pair 2: packet ___ and packet ___. Found by ___
Pair 3: packet ___ and packet ___. Found by ___
Pair 4: packet ___ and packet ___. Found by ___

rules: A grown-up is the packer. The packer cuts eight paper squares about 8 centimetres wide from a notebook page.

The packer puts a smell on each square and folds it shut. Two squares get one crushed clove each. Two get a pinch of cumin seeds (jeera). Two get a pinch of coffee or tea powder. Two get one crushed cardamom pod (elaichi).
The packer sticks a letter on each packet and secretly writes down which letters are pairs. Then the packer lays the packets in two rows.
On your turn, pick up two packets and sniff each one. Do not open them.
If you think they smell the same, say 'nestmates'. The packer checks the list. If you are right, keep the pair and take another turn.
If you are wrong, or if you say 'strangers', put both packets back in their places. Then the next player has a turn.
The game ends when all four pairs are found. The player with the most pairs wins. If you play alone, count your turns and try to use fewer next time.

flow.do: Make the eight packets where the players cannot see. Stick on the labels A to H. Write down the four pairs and keep the list hidden.
flow.say: Ants in one nest all carry the same nest smell. An ant touches another ant with her antennae and knows at once: nestmate or stranger. These eight packets are eight ants from four nests.
flow.kid: Wait while a grown-up makes eight smell packets. Do not peek.
flow.parent: Fold each square in half twice so that nothing falls out. Any four kitchen smells that differ clearly will do, such as fennel, ajwain or dried ginger. Wash your hands before you stick on the labels, so that the outsides smell the same.
flow.context: This is the first step of Nestmate or Stranger. A grown-up makes the eight smell packets.

flow.do: Play the game by the rules until all four pairs are found. Fill in the score sheet.
flow.say: Pick up two packets. Sniff each one slowly. Are they nestmates or strangers? Remember where each smell lies, because the packets go back to the same places.
flow.kid: Sniff two packets. Same smell? Say 'nestmates'. Different? Put them back.
flow.parent: If a nose gets tired, the player can sniff their own sleeve for a moment and then go on.
flow.context: In this step of Nestmate or Stranger you sniff the packets and find the pairs.

flow.do: Open one packet of each smell and look inside. Talk about the questions below.
flow.say: You told four nests apart with your nose alone. What would happen to an ant who walked into the wrong nest? How do you think the guards would know?
flow.kid: Open the packets and look. How does an ant know a stranger?

ask.q: How does a guard ant know that a visitor is a stranger?
good: The stranger smells of a different nest.
She touches the visitor with her antennae and smells her.

check.q: How does an ant tell a nestmate from a stranger?
options: By the smell on the other ant's body
By the colour of the other ant
check.why: Each nest has its own smell, and every ant in the nest carries it. An ant smells another ant by touching her with the antennae. Picking colour may mean you were thinking of how people know each other by sight.

flow.context: This is the last step of Nestmate or Stranger. You talk about how ants use the nest smell.

experiments.title: The Smell Mark Test: how long does a smell message last?
experiments.question: A smell mark is left on paper and the sender goes away. Can a nose still find the mark after 10 minutes, after 30 minutes and after 60 minutes? Does a vinegar mark last as long as a clove mark?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. After one hour, will you still find the vinegar mark? Will you still find the clove mark? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same paper for all eight squares, and make every square the same size. Put the same amount of liquid on every square in the vinegar set: 5 drops of vinegar on one, and 5 drops of water on each of the other three. Keep both sets in the same room, away from the fan and the window. The same person sniffs every time, with eyes covered, and the squares come in a mixed-up order. Sniff the vinegar set first each time, because clove is strong. Only two things change: the kind of mark, and the time since it was made.
results_table: Minutes since the marks were made
Vinegar mark found? Try 1 and try 2
Clove mark found? Try 1 and try 2

materials.item: squares of plain notebook paper, each about 10 centimetres wide
vinegar, 5 drops (or 5 drops of fresh lemon juice if you have no vinegar)
whole clove (lavang)
steel spoon, to crush and rub the clove
steel plates or trays, one for each set of four squares
a cloth or dupatta to cover the eyes
a pencil, a clock or phone timer, and a notebook page for the results

experiments.record: Draw a table with four rows, for 0, 10, 30 and 60 minutes. For each time, write a tick or a cross for every try. There are two tries with the vinegar set and two with the clove set.
experiments.context: In this experiment you leave two smell marks on paper, one of vinegar and one of clove. Then you test with your nose how long each mark can still be found.

setup.art: Eight paper squares on a table in two sets of four, with small pencil numbers on the corners, a clove, a spoon and a small bowl of vinegar.
setup.caption: 1. Number the squares. Make two sets of four.

setup.art: A grown-up letting drops of vinegar fall from a spoon onto the middle of one paper square while a child looks away.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up puts 5 drops of vinegar on one square, where the child cannot see.

setup.art: A grown-up crushing a clove on the middle of another paper square with the back of a steel spoon.
setup.caption: 3. The grown-up crushes a clove on one square of the other set and rubs for 10 seconds.

setup.art: A child with a cloth over her eyes sniffing a paper square that a grown-up holds by one corner under her nose.
setup.caption: 4. With eyes covered, sniff each square. Say which one carries the mark.

setup.art: A notebook table with rows for 0, 10, 30 and 60 minutes and ticks and crosses in two columns.
setup.caption: 5. Test again at 10, 30 and 60 minutes. Write a tick or a cross each time.

flow.do: Show your child the vinegar and the clove. Let them sniff each once. Ask for the guess and the reason, and write both down.
flow.say: We will leave a vinegar mark on one paper square and a clove mark on another. Then we walk away. After one hour, will your nose still find the vinegar mark? Will it find the clove mark? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Sniff the vinegar and the clove. Which smell will last one hour? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think that mark will last longer?
good: Clove smells stronger.
Vinegar is wet and will dry up.
The clove leaves bits and oil on the paper.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. If you have no vinegar, use fresh lemon juice.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Smell Mark Test. You guess which smell mark will last longer, before you test.

flow.do: Write V1 to V4 on four squares and C1 to C4 on the other four. Send your child out. Put 5 drops of vinegar on one V square and 5 drops of water on the other three. Crush the clove on one C square with the spoon and rub for 10 seconds. Tip the clove bits into the bin. Note the two marked numbers and the time.
flow.say: Please wait outside for two minutes. I am the sender. I will mark one square in each set, and I will not tell you which.
flow.kid: Number the squares. Then wait outside. A grown-up marks one square in each set.
flow.parent: Put each set on its own plate, with the squares not touching. Keep the two plates about two metres apart. Use the spoon on the clove, not your fingers. Then your hands will not carry the smell to the plain squares. The water on the plain V squares makes all four equally damp.
flow.context: In this step of the Smell Mark Test a grown-up makes the vinegar mark and the clove mark in secret.

flow.do: Cover your child's eyes. Lift each V square by one corner, in a mixed-up order. Hold the middle about 2 centimetres under the nose for two slow breaths. Ask which of the four carried the mark. Do this twice. Then do the same with the C squares. Record ticks and crosses for 0 minutes.
flow.say: Eyes covered. I will bring four squares, one at a time. One of them carries the mark. Tell me if it is the first, second, third or fourth. You may also say that none of them smells.
flow.kid: Cover your eyes. Sniff four squares. Say which one has the smell.

check.q: Why are your eyes covered during the Smell Mark Test?
options: So only my nose can find the mark
check.why: A wet patch or a brown stain would show you the marked square. With your eyes covered, a right answer can only come from the smell. If you chose 'the smell gets stronger', remember that covering your eyes changes nothing about the paper.

flow.parent: By guessing alone, a child would be right about 1 time in 4. Two right answers out of two is good evidence that the mark can still be found.
flow.context: In this step of the Smell Mark Test you sniff the fresh vinegar and clove marks with your eyes covered.

flow.do: When 10 minutes have passed since marking, test both sets again, twice each, in a new mixed-up order. Record the results.
flow.say: Ten minutes have passed, and the sender has been away all that time. Eyes covered again. Vinegar set first.
flow.kid: Ten minutes have passed. Cover your eyes and sniff again.
flow.wait: Wait 10 minutes after the marks were made
flow.context: In this step of the Smell Mark Test you sniff both marks again, 10 minutes after they were made.

flow.do: When 30 minutes have passed since marking, test both sets again, twice each. Record the results.
flow.say: Thirty minutes now. Take two breaths of fresh air first. Then tell me which square carries the mark, or say none.
flow.kid: Thirty minutes have passed. Sniff both sets again.
flow.wait: Wait until 30 minutes after the marks were made
flow.parent: Use the waiting time for the term cards or the story. If your child says 'none', record a cross. That is a real result.
flow.context: In this step of the Smell Mark Test you sniff both marks 30 minutes after they were made.

flow.do: When 60 minutes have passed since marking, test both sets once more, twice each. Record the results. Then show your child which squares were marked.
flow.say: This is the last test, one hour after I made the marks. Vinegar set first, then clove.
flow.kid: One hour has passed. Sniff both sets once more.
flow.wait: Wait until 60 minutes after the marks were made
flow.context: In this step of the Smell Mark Test you sniff both marks one hour after they were made.

flow.do: Look at the table together. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they found, and why they think it happened. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Look at your ticks and crosses. Say what you thought would happen, what you found, and why you think it happened. Which mark would suit an alarm that must end quickly? Which would suit a mark that says 'I live here'?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you found. Say why.

ask.q: Why might one smell fade faster than another?
good: Its smell particles leave the paper faster.
It dried up.
The clove left oil that stays.

ask.q: The sender was out of the room. How did the message still reach you?
good: The smell stayed on the paper.
The mark does not need the sender to be there.

flow.parent: In most homes the vinegar mark is hard to find after 30 to 60 minutes. The clove mark is still clear the next morning. Write down what you really found, even if it differs. The reason: a smell is made of molecules that leave the paper and float into the nose. The molecules of vinegar's smell are small and leave quickly, so the mark soon runs out. Clove oil has heavier molecules that leave slowly, so the mark lasts. Animals use both kinds. In some ants an alarm pheromone fades in about a minute. A tiger's mark on a tree lasts for days. Leave the clove square out and sniff it again tomorrow.
flow.think: Where would an animal put a scent mark so that it lasts as long as possible?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Smell Mark Test. You say what your results show about the vinegar mark and the clove mark.

experiments.title: The Echo Plate Test: can you find a thing by sound alone?
experiments.question: Your eyes are covered. Can you tell whether a steel plate is in front of your face by saying 'shhh' and listening? Does it still work when the plate is 30 centimetres or 60 centimetres away?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. With your eyes covered, will you be able to tell when the plate is there? At which distance will it stop working: 10, 30 or 60 centimetres? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same plate, the same room and the same 'shhh' every time. Each round has 10 turns: 5 with the plate and 5 without, in a mixed-up order that the listener cannot know. The helper steps forward the same way on every turn, so that footsteps give nothing away. Keep the room quiet. Do one round at 10 centimetres with no 'shhh' at all, to check that the echo is what helps. Only the distance and the sound change.

materials.item: a large flat steel plate (thali), about 25 to 30 centimetres wide. A steel tray or a big hard-cover book also works
a cloth or dupatta to cover the eyes
a ruler or measuring tape
a pencil and a notebook page for the results

experiments.record: Draw a table with four rows, one for each round. Write the distance, whether you made the 'shhh' sound, and how many of the 10 answers were right.
experiments.context: In this experiment you cover your eyes and say 'shhh'. You try to tell whether a steel plate is in front of your face. Bats and dolphins find things in a similar way.

setup.art: A child sitting on a chair saying 'shhh' and moving a steel plate slowly towards her own face with her eyes open.
setup.caption: 1. Practise first. Say 'shhh' and move the plate towards your face. Listen to the sound change.

setup.art: The child with a cloth over her eyes saying 'shhh', and a grown-up holding a steel plate upright a short way in front of her face.
setup.caption: 2. Cover your eyes. On some turns the helper holds the plate in front of you.

setup.art: The same child with covered eyes, and the grown-up standing in the same place with the plate hidden behind their back.
setup.caption: 3. On other turns the helper keeps the plate behind their back. Say 'plate' or 'no plate'.

setup.art: A notebook table with four rows: 10 centimetres, 30 centimetres, 60 centimetres, and 10 centimetres with no sound, each with a score out of 10.
setup.caption: 4. Do 10 turns at each distance. Then do 10 turns with no sound. Write each score.

flow.do: Show your child the plate and the cloth. Explain the test. Ask for the guess and the reason, and write both down.
flow.say: You will cover your eyes and say a long 'shhh'. Sometimes I will hold this plate in front of your face, and sometimes I will not. Will you be able to tell? Up to what distance? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Your eyes will be covered. Can you tell when a plate is near? Why?

ask.q: What could tell you that the plate is there?
good: The 'shhh' might sound different.
The sound might bounce back.
I might feel the air change.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Children often say they will feel the plate. The last round tests that idea.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Echo Plate Test. You guess whether you can find a plate by sound, before you test.

flow.do: Let your child hold the plate with eyes open. They say a steady, loud 'shhh'. They move the plate slowly from arm's length to 5 centimetres from the mouth, and back. Do this five times.
flow.say: Keep your 'shhh' steady, like air leaking from a tyre. Move the plate slowly towards your mouth and away again. Listen hard. Does anything about the sound change?
flow.kid: Say 'shhh'. Move the plate close, then away. Listen for a change.
flow.parent: Most people hear the 'shhh' become sharper or more hollow when the plate is within about 20 centimetres. Let your child find their own words for the change. A quick tongue click also works, if your child prefers it.
flow.context: In this step of the Echo Plate Test you practise with your eyes open. You learn how the 'shhh' changes near the plate.

flow.do: Round 1, at 10 centimetres. Write P five times and N five times in a mixed-up order. Cover your child's eyes. On each turn they start the 'shhh'. Step forward. On P turns hold the plate upright 10 centimetres from the face. On N turns keep it behind your back. Count three, ask 'plate or no plate?', and step back. Record each answer.
flow.say: Round 1. Start your 'shhh' when I say go. I will step forward every time. Tell me 'plate' or 'no plate'. Go.
flow.kid: Round 1. Say 'shhh'. Listen. Say 'plate' or 'no plate'.
flow.parent: Measure 10 centimetres once with the ruler, and then judge it by eye. Do not let the plate touch hair or clothes. Do not say whether each answer is right until the round ends.
flow.context: In this step of the Echo Plate Test you do 10 turns with the plate 10 centimetres from your face.

flow.do: Round 2, at 30 centimetres. Write a new mixed-up order of five P and five N. Do 10 turns the same way and record the score.
flow.say: Round 2. The plate will now be further away, about as long as your ruler. Same rules. Go.
flow.kid: Round 2. The plate is further away now. Listen carefully.
flow.context: In this step of the Echo Plate Test you do 10 turns with the plate 30 centimetres from your face.

flow.do: Round 3, at 60 centimetres. Write a new mixed-up order. Do 10 turns the same way and record the score.
flow.say: Round 3. The plate will be two ruler lengths away. It may be hard. Give your best answer every time.
flow.kid: Round 3. The plate is far now. Give your best answer.
flow.context: In this step of the Echo Plate Test you do 10 turns with the plate 60 centimetres from your face.

flow.do: Round 4, at 10 centimetres with no sound. Your child keeps their mouth closed and stays silent. Do 10 turns in a new mixed-up order and record the score.
flow.say: Round 4. The plate is back at 10 centimetres. This time make no sound at all. Keep your mouth closed. Tell me 'plate' or 'no plate'.
flow.kid: Round 4. Make no sound this time. Say 'plate' or 'no plate'.

check.q: Why does the Echo Plate Test have one round with no 'shhh' sound?
options: To check that the echo is what helps
To give my voice a rest
check.why: Suppose you score well with the 'shhh' and only about 5 out of 10 in silence. Then the echo was what told you. If you also score well in silence, something else is helping. It may be warm air or small noises in the room.

flow.context: In this step of the Echo Plate Test you do 10 turns at 10 centimetres without making the 'shhh' sound.

flow.do: Look at the four scores together. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they found, and why they think it happened. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Guessing alone gives about 5 right out of 10. Look at your four scores. Say what you thought would happen, what you found, and why you think it happened.
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you found. Say why.

ask.q: Which scores are clearly better than guessing?
good: The ones well above 5 out of 10.
The 10 centimetre round with 'shhh'.

ask.q: Why might the far plate be harder to find?
good: The echo is weaker.
The echo mixes with the echoes from the walls.

flow.parent: With the 'shhh', many people score 8 to 10 at 10 centimetres and less at 30 centimetres. At 60 centimetres and in silence, most score about 5. Write down what you really found. The reason: the 'shhh' bounces off the plate and returns to the ears, mixed with the sound coming straight from the mouth. The mix sounds different from the 'shhh' alone. From further away the echo is weaker, and a room's own echoes hide it. A bat does the same thing far better. She uses short, loud calls and large ears, and her brain times each echo.
flow.think: A bat can find a moth several metres away. What does she have that you do not?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Echo Plate Test. You say what your four scores show.

activities.title: Signal Spotting: ten minutes at the window

materials.item: a notebook page and a pencil
a window, a balcony or a doorway that looks on to a street or a yard

schedule.what: Watch for five minutes and count the signals on each channel.

activities.record: A table with four rows: smell, sight, sound and touch. Put one stroke for every signal you notice. Write who sent each one if you can.
activities.context: In this activity you watch people, birds, dogs and insects for five minutes. You count the signals they send by smell, sight, sound and touch.

setup.art: A notebook page with a table of four rows labelled Smell, Sight, Sound and Touch.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a table with four rows: smell, sight, sound and touch.

setup.art: A child at a window looking down at a street with two dogs, a crow on a wire and people talking at a tea stall.
setup.caption: 2. Watch for five minutes. Humans count too.

setup.art: The notebook page with strokes in the rows, most of them next to Sound and Sight.
setup.caption: 3. Put one stroke in the right row for each signal.

flow.do: Draw the table with four rows. Choose a place to watch from. If the street is empty, watch your own family.
flow.say: A signal is anything one animal does that carries a message to another. Humans are animals, so our waves, horns and hugs count. Which row do you think will fill up fastest?
flow.kid: Draw four rows: smell, sight, sound, touch. Which will get the most strokes?
flow.context: This is the first step of Signal Spotting. You draw the table and guess which channel you will see most.

flow.do: Watch for five minutes. Each time anyone sends a signal, your child says what it was and puts a stroke in the right row.
flow.say: Tell me each signal as you spot it. A crow calling is sound. A person waving is sight. A dog sniffing a wall is smell. A mother holding a child's hand is touch.
flow.kid: Watch for five minutes. Put a stroke for every signal.
flow.parent: There is no garden needed. A street, a corridor or your own kitchen will give plenty of signals. Do not worry about missing some.
flow.context: In this step of Signal Spotting you watch for five minutes and count each signal by channel.

flow.do: Count the strokes in each row. Talk about the questions below.
flow.say: Which row has the most strokes? Which has the fewest? Do you think there were really so few smell signals, or did we miss them?
flow.kid: Count each row. Which channel won? Which signals did you miss?

ask.q: Why is the smell row nearly empty?
good: Our noses are not good enough to notice them.
We cannot see a smell.
The dog noticed smells that we missed.

flow.parent: The count shows what a human watcher can notice. A dog at the same window would fill the smell row first.
flow.context: This is the last step of Signal Spotting. You count the strokes and ask which signals you could not notice.

activities.title: Three Strings: feel a message the way a spider does

materials.item: pieces of thin string, wool or strong thread, each about 2 metres long
chairs, door handles or window bars to tie the far ends to
a pencil for plucking

schedule.what: Tie three strings, feel which one is plucked, then send a code.

activities.record: Write how many of the 9 plucks you named correctly. Then write the two codes you used and whether they were understood.
activities.context: In this activity you hold three tight strings with your eyes shut. You feel which string is plucked, the way a spider feels which thread of her web is shaking.

setup.art: Three long strings tied to three different chairs, all meeting at one child's hand like the spokes of a wheel.
setup.caption: 1. Tie three strings to three chairs. Bring the free ends together.

setup.art: A close view of a hand with one string looped round each of three fingers, all pulled tight.
setup.caption: 2. Loop one string round each of three fingers. Pull them tight.

setup.art: A grown-up plucking one string near a chair with a pencil while the child, eyes shut, points with the other hand.
setup.caption: 3. Shut your eyes. A helper plucks one string. Say which one.

flow.do: Tie one end of each string to a different chair. Bring the three free ends to one spot. Your child loops one string round each of three fingers: the first, the middle and the ring finger. They pull all three tight.
flow.say: A spider sits at the middle of her web with her feet on the threads. You are the spider. Your three fingers are three of her feet. Keep the strings tight.
flow.kid: Loop one string on each of three fingers. Pull them tight.
flow.context: This is the first step of Three Strings. You set up three tight strings that meet at your hand.

flow.do: Your child shuts their eyes. Pluck one string gently near the chair with the pencil. Your child says which finger felt it. Do 9 plucks, three on each string in a mixed-up order. Count the right answers.
flow.say: Eyes shut. I will pluck one string. Tell me which finger felt it most: first, middle or ring.
flow.kid: Shut your eyes. Feel the pluck. Say which finger felt it.
flow.parent: The plucked string shakes much more than the other two, so most children get 8 or 9 right. Pluck softly and walk quietly.
flow.context: In this step of Three Strings you feel, with your eyes shut, which of the three strings was plucked.

flow.do: Agree two codes: one slow pluck means 'wind', and three quick plucks means 'fly'. Send six messages in a mixed-up order on any string. Your child names the string and the message. Then swap places.
flow.say: A spider must tell a trapped fly from the wind. A fly struggles in quick bursts. Now each pluck has a meaning. One slow pluck is wind. Three quick plucks are a fly.
flow.kid: One slow pluck means wind. Three quick plucks mean fly. Which is this?
flow.context: In this step of Three Strings the plucks carry a code. You read the code with your eyes shut.

flow.do: Put the strings down. Talk about the questions below.
flow.say: You could not see or hear the message, yet you read it. What carried it? Could I have sent it if you had let go of the strings?
flow.kid: What carried the message to your fingers? What if you let go?

ask.q: What does a vibration signal need that a call does not?
good: Something that joins the sender and the receiver.
A thread, a stem or the ground between them.

check.q: A spider is at the middle of her web. How does she know where a trapped fly is?
options: She feels which thread is shaking most
check.why: The fly shakes the threads nearest to them, and those threads shake the spider's feet most. In Three Strings your finger on the plucked string felt the most shaking in the same way.

flow.context: This is the last step of Three Strings. You talk about how a vibration carried the message along the string.

activities.title: The Waving Test: how big must a signal be?

materials.item: a bright cloth, such as a yellow or red dupatta or towel
the longest room or corridor in your home
a notebook page and a pencil

schedule.what: Send three movements at three sizes across a dim room, and count how many are read correctly.

activities.record: A table with three rows: one finger, whole hand, and arm with a bright cloth. Write how many of the 3 signals were read correctly for each.
activities.context: In this activity a sender stands at the far end of a dim room and makes a movement. You find out how big and bright the movement must be for the receiver to read it.

setup.art: A long dim corridor with a child at one end and a grown-up at the other end, about ten steps apart.
setup.caption: 1. Stand at the two ends of your longest room. Make the room dim.

setup.art: Three small drawings of an arm: moving up and down, moving side to side, and drawing a circle.
setup.caption: 2. Agree three movements: up and down, side to side, and a circle.

setup.art: A grown-up at the far end of the corridor sweeping a bright yellow cloth in a circle.
setup.caption: 3. Send each movement with one finger, then a hand, then an arm with a bright cloth.

flow.do: Draw the curtains or switch off the lights so that the room is dim but safe to walk in. Stand at the two ends. Agree the three movements. Ask for a guess.
flow.say: A fiddler crab waves a huge claw, and a peacock raises a huge train. Why so big? We will send three movements with a finger, a hand and a whole arm with a cloth. Which will you read most easily, and why?
flow.kid: We will send signals across a dim room. Which size will be easiest? Why?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Waving Test. You set up a dim room and guess which size of signal will be read best.

flow.do: The sender shows each signal for a count of two. Send three with one finger, three with the whole hand and three with the arm and cloth. Mix up the movements. The receiver calls out what they saw. Record right or wrong. Then swap places.
flow.say: Watch me. I will show each movement only for a count of two. Call out 'up and down', 'side to side' or 'circle'.
flow.kid: Watch the sender. Call out the movement you saw.
flow.parent: If every signal is easy to read, make the room dimmer or stand further apart. The corridor outside your flat may be longer. The finger signals should become hard first.
flow.context: In this step of the Waving Test the sender makes each movement at three sizes. The receiver calls out what they saw.

flow.do: Compare the three rows. Talk about the questions below.
flow.say: Which size did you read best? A big bright signal is easy for a mate to see. Who else can see it easily?
flow.kid: Which size worked best? Who else could see a big signal?

ask.q: What is the danger of a big, bright signal?
good: A hunter can see it too.
It takes more energy.

check.q: Why does a male fiddler crab wave his biggest claw, and not a small leg?
options: A big thing is seen from far away
check.why: In the Waving Test, bigger signals are usually read from further away than small ones. A big claw works the same way on a wide mudflat.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Waving Test. You compare the three sizes of signal and ask what a big signal costs.

projects.title: Our Family Signal Code: six signals in three days

materials.item: a notebook page for the code and the log
a bright cloth, a spoon and a steel tumbler, or other things you choose for your signals
a pencil

schedule.what: Invent six signals and teach them to your family.
Use the signals all day and log each one.
Count which signals worked, and change the ones that failed.

projects.record: A code page with six signals and their meanings. A log with one line for each time a signal was sent: which signal, where, and whether it was understood.
projects.context: In this three-day project your family invents six signals with no words. You use them for a day and find out which ones work.

setup.art: A notebook page titled Our Code with six rows, each with a small drawing of a signal and its meaning.
setup.caption: 1. Invent six signals. Use sight, sound and touch, with no words.

setup.art: A child tapping a spoon on a steel tumbler in a kitchen while a parent in the next room looks up.
setup.caption: 2. Use the signals for a whole day. Log each one.

setup.art: A log page with ticks and crosses next to each signal, and one signal circled.
setup.caption: 3. Count the ticks. Change the signals that failed.

flow.do: Day 1. Choose six messages your family often needs. Some ideas are 'food is ready', 'come here', 'I need help', 'be quiet', 'yes' and 'no'. Invent one signal without words for each. Use at least three channels. Write the code and teach it to everyone at home.
flow.say: We need six signals with no words. Some must work when the receiver is in another room. Some must work when the mixer is running. Which channel suits each message?
flow.kid: Invent six signals with no words. Use sight, sound and touch.
flow.parent: Good codes mix channels: two taps on a tumbler, a cloth hung on a door handle, a squeeze of the hand. Let your child choose, even if a signal looks likely to fail. Finding out is the point.
flow.context: This is day 1 of Our Family Signal Code. You invent six signals and teach them to your family.

flow.do: Day 2. Use the signals through the day instead of words, whenever you can. After each one, write a line in the log: the signal, where the receiver was, and a tick if it was understood.
flow.say: Today we use the code. After every signal, we log whether it was understood. A signal that fails is as useful to us as one that works.
flow.kid: Use your signals all day. Log a tick or a cross each time.
flow.wait: Do this the day after you invent the code
flow.context: This is day 2 of Our Family Signal Code. You use your six signals and log whether each was understood.

flow.do: Day 3. Count the ticks and crosses for each signal. For each failure, work out why: was it missed, or mixed up with another signal? Change the signals that failed and say why the new ones should work better.
flow.say: Which signal worked every time? Which failed? Was it too small, too quiet, or too much like another one? Animals with signals that fail do not get fed or found. What would you change?
flow.kid: Count the ticks. Which signal failed? Why? Make it better.
flow.wait: Do this on the third day

ask.q: What made your best signal work so well?
good: It was big or loud enough to notice.
It was different from all the others.
It worked even when the receiver was not looking.

flow.context: This is day 3 of Our Family Signal Code. You count which signals worked and improve the ones that failed.

challenges.title: Message Through the Noise: reach a listener who cannot hear you
challenges.problem: A dancing frog lives beside a stream so loud that his call is often lost. He adds a second signal: a white foot. Your problem is like his. A receiver sits five big steps away, facing a wall, with music playing. Send them one of three messages, 'come', 'stay' or 'danger', so that they get it right every time.
constraints: The receiver faces the wall and does not turn round.
Music or a mixer is on the whole time.
The sender stays five big steps away.
The receiver must name the message within 10 seconds.
materials: a long piece of string or wool, about 5 metres
a steel plate and a spoon
a few sheets of old newspaper
a phone or radio to play music
a chair for the receiver, facing a wall
general: Shine a torch on the wall in front of the receiver, with one, two or three flashes.
Tie a string to the receiver's wrist or chair and send tugs along it.
Stamp on the floor so that the receiver feels it through their feet.
creative: Make shadow shapes on the receiver's wall with a torch and your hand: a different shape for each message.
Use two channels together, such as tugs and flashes, so that the message arrives even if one channel fails.
Roll a ball of newspaper past the receiver's feet: one ball, two balls or three.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own way. It must still work if the lights go out, or if someone trips over the string. Draw your design. Test it with 9 messages in a mixed-up order, and write how many the receiver got right.
challenges.context: In this challenge you must get a message to someone who cannot hear you and is not looking at you. It is the problem a dancing frog solves beside a loud stream.

setup.art: A child sitting on a chair facing a wall with a radio playing beside her, and another child five steps behind her holding a torch and a ball of string.
setup.caption: 1. The receiver faces a wall, with music on. The sender stands five big steps away.

setup.art: A torch beam making a bright spot on the wall in front of the seated child.
setup.caption: 2. Try a signal that does not need ears or a turned head.

setup.art: A notebook page with nine messages listed and ticks beside most of them.
setup.caption: 3. Send 9 messages in a mixed-up order. Count how many arrive correctly.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Set up the chair, the wall and the music. Ask which channels are blocked and which are still open.
flow.say: The receiver cannot hear you and is not looking at you. Which channels are blocked? Which are still open? List every idea, even odd ones.
flow.kid: The receiver cannot hear or see you. Which channels are left?

ask.q: Which channels can still reach the receiver?
good: Touch, through a string or the floor.
Sight, if the signal lands on the wall in front of them.
Smell, but it would be slow.

flow.parent: Keep the music at a normal volume. It only needs to cover a tap or a whisper.
flow.context: This is the first step of Message Through the Noise. You work out which channels are blocked and which are open.

flow.do: Your child chooses one idea and builds it. Agree a code for the three messages: 'come', 'stay' and 'danger'.
flow.say: Choose your best idea and build it. The three messages must be easy to tell apart. How will 'danger' differ from 'come'?
flow.kid: Build your best idea. Make three signals that differ clearly.
flow.context: In this step of Message Through the Noise you build your signal and agree a code for three messages.

flow.do: Test it. Send 9 messages, three of each kind, in a mixed-up order. The receiver calls out each message within 10 seconds. Record right or wrong.
flow.say: Now we test. I will send nine messages. Call out each one as soon as you know it.
flow.kid: Test it with nine messages. Count how many arrive correctly.
flow.context: In this step of Message Through the Noise you test your signal with 9 messages and count the right answers.

flow.do: Look at the score. Change one thing to make it better, or add a second channel. Test three more messages. Then talk about the question below.
flow.say: Which messages went wrong, and why? Change one thing and try again. Would your signal still work in the dark?
flow.kid: What went wrong? Change one thing. Test it again.

ask.q: Why might an animal use two channels for one message?
good: If one channel is blocked, the other still gets through.
Two signals together are harder to miss.

flow.parent: Praise a clear account of what failed as much as a high score.
flow.context: This is the last step of Message Through the Noise. You improve your signal and test it again.

items.p: What is a signal?
opts: Something an animal does that carries a message
Any loud noise in a forest
A kind of animal that lives in groups
The food an animal carries home
items.why: A signal carries a message from a sender to a receiver. It can be a smell, a colour, a movement, a sound or a touch. It does not have to be loud.

items.p: Which body part does a male moth use to pick up a female's pheromone?
items.why: A male moth's feathery antennae are covered with tiny hairs that catch the pheromone from the air. If you chose eyes, remember that moths find mates in the dark.

items.p: A chemical that an animal gives off, which changes what others of the same kind do, is called a ____.
items.why: A pheromone is a smell signal made of one or more chemicals. Silk moths, ants and honeybees all use pheromones.

items.p: All bats are blind.
items.why: False. Every kind of bat has working eyes. Large fruit bats find food mainly by sight and smell. Small bats echolocate as well as see.

items.p: Match each signal to its channel.
pairs: A lizard flicks out a bright throat fan
A cricket rubs his wings together
A macaque picks through her friend's fur
items.why: Ask which body part of the receiver picks the signal up. A nose picks up the spray, an eye the fan, an ear the cricket's song, and skin the grooming.

items.p: Sort these signals. Does each one work in the dark, or does it need light?
items: a scent mark on a tree
items.why: Smells and sounds do not need light. Colours and displays are picked up by eyes, and eyes need light.

items.p: In the Smell Mark Test, three plain squares got 5 drops of water. Why?
opts: So all four squares were equally damp
So the paper would not burn
items.why: A fair test changes only one thing. With water on the plain squares, the only difference between the four squares was the smell of vinegar.

items.p: A scent mark can be read after the animal who made it has gone away.
items.why: True. The smell stays on the tree or the wall. That is what makes a scent mark different from a call or a wave.

items.p: Put these steps in order, to show how a bat finds a moth.
items: The bat makes a short, high call
The sound travels out to the moth
The sound bounces off the moth
The echo reaches the bat's ears
The bat turns towards the moth
a: The bat makes a short, high call
The sound travels out to the moth
The sound bounces off the moth
The echo reaches the bat's ears
The bat turns towards the moth
items.why: Echolocation is a call followed by an echo. The bat can only turn towards the moth after the echo has come back.

items.p: Sound that is too high for human ears to hear is called ____.
items.why: Ultrasound is above the highest sound we can hear. Most bats call in ultrasound. Sound too low for us is called infrasound.

items.p: How does a spider at the middle of her web know that a fly has landed?
items.why: A struggling fly makes the threads vibrate, and the spider feels this through her feet. This is the touch channel, carried by the web.

items.p: Explain in two sentences why a peacock's display would not work on a dark night.
items.a: A display is a signal for the eyes, and eyes need light. On a dark night the peahen could not see the colours or the shaking train. So the message would not reach her.
items.why: A strong answer says that the display travels on the sight channel, and that this channel needs light.

items.p: In the Smell Mark Test the sender was out of the room. Explain how the message still reached the receiver.
items.a: The sender left a smell on the paper. The smell stayed there after the sender had gone, and my nose picked it up later.
items.why: A strong answer says that the signal was left on a surface. So the sender did not need to be there when it was received.

items.p: Draw a bat's call going out to a moth and the echo coming back. Label the call and the echo.
items.a: A bat and a moth with one arrow from the bat's mouth to the moth, labelled 'call', and one arrow from the moth back to the bat's ears, labelled 'echo'.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the sound going both ways. The echo must start at the moth and end at the bat's ears.
items.art: A blank box with a small outline of a bat on the left and a moth on the right.

items.p: Which signal could reach an elephant family three kilometres away?
items.why: Low sounds travel far. Elephant rumbles can reach other elephants several kilometres away. A touch needs contact, and a flap or a raised tail must be seen.

items.p: A frog beside a loud stream calls and waves a white foot. Why does he wave?
opts: The stream's noise hides his call
items.why: Noise blocks the sound channel but not the sight channel. A second signal on another channel gets the message through.

items.p: An alarm pheromone fades after about a minute. Why is that useful?
opts: The alarm ends soon after the danger ends
It saves the animal from making smells
It makes the nest smell nicer
items.why: An alarm that stayed for days would keep the nest fighting an enemy who had gone. A fast-fading smell suits a short message.

items.p: A child scores 9 out of 10 with 'shhh' and 5 out of 10 in silence. What does this show?
opts: The echo of the 'shhh' was helping
items.why: Guessing gives about 5 out of 10. The score rose well above that only when there was a sound to bounce off the plate.

items.p: A tiger moth hears a bat's call and dives to the ground. What is the moth doing?
items.why: The bat's call was not meant for the moth. Picking up a signal meant for someone else is eavesdropping.

items.p: Echolocation is a message that a bat sends to a moth.
items.why: False. The bat is both the sender and the receiver. She calls in order to hear her own echoes. The moth only overhears.

items.p: Elephants make sounds that are too low for humans to hear.
items.why: True. Part of an elephant's rumble is infrasound, which is below the lowest sound human ears can hear.

items.p: Sort these signals. Does each one last after the sender leaves, or end when the sender stops?
items: a tigress's spray on a tree
a cat's cheek rub on a chair
items.why: Smell marks stay on a surface. Sounds and displays stop as soon as the sender stops making them.

items.p: Three of these signals travel on the sight channel. Which one is the odd one out?
items.why: The train, the fan and the claw are displays for the eyes. A cricket's song is a sound.

items.p: Sound travels 340 metres in one second. A cliff's echo returns after 2 seconds. How many metres away is the cliff?
items.why: In 2 seconds the sound travels 680 metres. That is the way there and the way back. Half of 680 is 340 metres.

items.p: Put the steps of the Smell Mark Test in order.
items: A grown-up marks one square in each set in secret
Sniff each square in a mixed-up order
Write a tick or a cross
a: A grown-up marks one square in each set in secret
Sniff each square in a mixed-up order
Write a tick or a cross
items.why: The marks are made in secret before any sniffing. The eyes are covered before the squares come, and each result is written before the next test.

items.p: The Ganges river dolphin is almost blind. Explain why this is not a problem for her in a muddy river.
items.a: Light does not pass through muddy water, so even good eyes would see very little. Sound travels well in water, so she clicks and uses the echoes to find fish.
items.why: A strong answer says why sight fails in mud, and that echoes do the job that eyes would do.

items.p: Write one gain and one cost of a big, bright display.
items.a: Gain: a mate or a rival can see it from far away. Cost: a hunter can see it too, or it takes a lot of energy to grow and to show.
items.why: A strong answer gives a real gain for the sender and a real cost. In the Waving Test, the biggest signal is usually the easiest to read from far away.

items.p: A watcher counts 20 signals, and only 1 is a smell. Why may the smell count be too low?
items.a: A human nose misses most smell signals, and smells cannot be seen from a window. The dogs and ants outside were probably sending and reading many more.
items.why: A strong answer sees that the count depends on the watcher's own senses. A count of what we noticed is not a count of what was there.

items.p: A busy road runs through a forest where frogs breed. People are deciding whether to stop lorries on monsoon nights.

views.says: Lorry noise hides the males' calls. If females cannot find males, there will be fewer frogs each year.
Night is when the road is clear. If I cannot drive at night, vegetables reach the market late and I earn less.
The road brings our ambulance and our bus. But the frogs eat the insects in our fields. Slow the lorries down, and keep the road open.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason, using what you know about sound signals. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason from the unit. One reason is that a call is lost in noise. Another is that frogs call only on some nights, so a rule for those nights could be enough.
items.why: Each view has something right in it. A strong answer uses the fact that noise blocks the sound channel, and takes the other needs seriously.

items.p: Label three parts of this dolphin's head: where clicks are made, the forehead's pad of fat, and the lower jaw.
labels: The pad of fat in the forehead
a: Where the clicks are made: the nose passages, just below the blowhole
The pad of fat in the forehead: it aims the clicks forward
The lower jaw: the echoes come in through it and pass to the ears
items.why: A dolphin sends clicks out through her forehead and takes the echoes in through her jaw. Sound goes out by one path and comes back by another.
items.art: A side view of a dolphin's head showing the blowhole on top, the rounded forehead and the long lower jaw, with three blank label lines.

items.p: A male moth sees a female, but his antennae are covered. He fails to find her. What does this show?
opts: He was not looking for her
items.why: With his eyes working and his antennae covered, he fails. So the antennae, which pick up smell, are what he needs.

items.p: Suppose most of a drongo's alarm calls were false. What would probably happen?
opts: The drongo would lose their voice
items.why: A false signal only works while most signals are true. Receivers who are fooled too often learn to ignore the call.

items.p: A bat hears the echo from thing A sooner than the echo from thing B. What does she learn?
items.why: Sound takes time to travel. An echo that comes back sooner has made a shorter trip, so the thing is nearer.

items.p: Does a frog's foot wave work without his call? Which test would show this best?
opts: Show frogs a silent model foot that waves
Count the frogs at the stream
items.why: To test the wave alone, the call must be taken away. A silent model that only waves changes one thing, which makes the test fair.

items.p: A signal reaches only the animal that the sender meant it for.
items.why: False. A call or a smell spreads out, and any animal with the right senses can pick it up. Bats hunt frogs by their calls.

items.p: Large fruit bats, such as the Indian flying fox, find fruit mainly with their eyes and noses.
items.why: True. Large fruit bats do not echolocate. Small insect-eating bats do.

items.p: Match each place to a signal that works well there.
pairs: A thick forest at night, after the sender has left
An open mudflat in bright sun
items.why: Each place blocks some channels and leaves others open. Darkness blocks sight, mud blocks sight, and open sunny ground suits a display.

items.p: The Echo Plate Test has 40 turns in all. Guessing gets about half right. How many is that?
items.why: The test has 4 rounds of 10 turns, which is 40 turns. Half of 40 is 20. A total well above 20 shows that something more than guessing was at work.

items.p: Picking up a signal that was meant for someone else is called ____.
items.why: A bat who hunts a calling frog and a moth who hears a bat are both eavesdropping.

items.p: A score of 6 out of 10 in the Echo Plate Test: is that good evidence of hearing the echo? Explain.
items.a: No, it is weak evidence. Guessing gives about 5 out of 10, and 6 is only one more. More turns would be needed to be sure.
items.why: A strong answer compares the score with what guessing would give, and asks for more turns before deciding.

items.p: Many animals of the night use smell and sound, and few use colour. Explain why, with one example.
items.a: Colours need light, and there is little light at night. Smells and sounds work in the dark. For example, a female moth draws males with a pheromone.
items.why: A strong answer links the channel to the conditions, and gives a real night animal as the example.

items.p: How is a scent mark like a written note? How is it different?
items.a: Both stay behind and give their message when the sender is away. They differ because a note can say many different things. A scent mark says a few things, such as who was here and when.
items.why: A strong answer names the lasting of the message as the likeness. Any sensible difference is accepted.

items.p: Why does a vinegar mark usually fade sooner than a clove mark? Use the word molecules.
items.a: A smell is made of molecules that leave the paper and float to the nose. Vinegar's smell molecules are small and leave quickly, so they are soon used up. Clove oil's molecules are heavier and leave slowly, so the mark lasts.
items.why: A strong answer says that a smell is molecules leaving a surface. The mark ends when few are left.

items.p: A monkey gives an alarm call, and the other monkeys climb a tree. Scientists describe what happened in different ways.

views.says: The call carries information. It tells the listeners that a leopard is near, and they decide to climb.
The call is a way of making the others move. We should ask what the call makes them do, and whom that helps.
Both are right. The caller has reasons to call, and each listener weighs the call and chooses.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason from this unit. Then say what test might help to decide.
items.a: Any view with a reason. One reason is that monkeys respond differently to different calls. Another is that false alarm calls show a signal can be used to push others.
items.why: Working scientists hold each of these views. A strong answer uses an example from the unit and suggests a test, such as playing a call from a hidden speaker.

items.p: Draw an animal signalling in a dark forest or beside a loud stream. Name the channel and why it fits.
items.a: For example, a moth in a night forest giving off a pheromone, with the note: 'Smell, because it works in the dark and goes round trees.'
items.why: A strong drawing matches the channel to the place: a display fails in the dark, and a quiet call fails beside a loud stream.
items.art: A blank box with two small corner sketches: a moon over trees and a rushing stream.

quiz.p: Which list names the four channels of animal signals?
quiz.why: A channel is the way a signal travels. Eyes and ears are body parts that receive signals, and barks and purrs are all on one channel, sound.

opts: A chemical signal between animals of one kind
quiz.why: A pheromone is a chemical that an animal gives off, which changes what others of the same kind do. It travels on the smell channel.

quiz.p: Why is a scent mark on a tree useful to a tigress?
opts: It works while she is far away
It can be changed in a second
quiz.why: A smell stays on the bark for days. So the mark tells other tigers she lives here, even while she hunts elsewhere. A smell cannot be changed quickly.

quiz.p: In the Smell Mark Test, the squares came in a mixed-up order. Why?
opts: So I could not guess from the order
quiz.why: If the marked square always came third, you could answer without smelling. A mixed-up order means only your nose can find the mark.

quiz.p: Which of these blocks a display but does not block a call?
quiz.why: A display needs light. A call needs no light, so it works at night. Loud noise does the opposite: it blocks a call and leaves a display clear.

quiz.p: What do the orange and black wings of a plain tiger butterfly tell a bird?
quiz.why: These are warning colours. A bird who has tried one such butterfly remembers the colours and leaves the next one alone.

quiz.p: What is sound too low for human ears called?
quiz.why: Infrasound is below our hearing, and elephants use it. Ultrasound is above our hearing, and bats use it.

quiz.p: Why is a call a good way to raise an alarm?
opts: It is fast and spreads all round
quiz.why: A call reaches everyone nearby at once, even behind trees and in the dark. It can stop as soon as the danger ends. Hunters can hear it too, which is its cost.

quiz.p: Which signal needs the sender and the receiver to touch the same thing?
opts: A pluck on a spider's web
quiz.why: A vibration travels along the thread, so both spiders must be on the web. Calls, displays and pheromones cross open air.

quiz.p: How does a bat know how far away a moth is?
opts: By how soon the echo comes back
quiz.why: Sound takes time to travel. The longer the echo takes to return, the further away the moth is.

quiz.p: Why does a Ganges river dolphin find fish by echoes and not by sight?
opts: Muddy water blocks light but not sound
Fish are too small to see
Her eyes are on her back
quiz.why: Light cannot pass through muddy water, so eyes are little use there. Sound travels well in water, so echoes work.

quiz.p: A male frog's call draws a female. It also draws a hunting bat. What is the bat doing?
quiz.why: The call was meant for female frogs. The bat picks up a signal meant for someone else, which is eavesdropping.

videos.why: To hear how a bat's calls come faster and faster as she closes in on an insect.

applications: Farmers hang pheromone traps in cotton, vegetable and coconut fields. The trap gives off an insect pheromone, so the insects fly in, and the farmer sprays less poison.
Ships and fishing boats use sonar. The machine sends a sound into the water and times the echo, as a dolphin does.
A hospital ultrasound scan sends very high sound into the body and builds a picture from the echoes.
Sniffer dogs at airports and railway stations find things by smells that people cannot notice.
Road signs, school buses and auto-rickshaws use yellow and black, because these colours are easy to see. Wasps wear the same warning colours.
Some blind people find their way by clicking their tongues. They listen to the echoes from walls, doors and parked cars.

open_questions.q: What do the songs of humpback whales mean?
open_questions.why_open: Only males sing, and all the males in one area sing the same song, which slowly changes. Scientists do not agree on what the song tells other whales.

open_questions.q: What are sperm whales saying with their patterns of clicks?
open_questions.why_open: Sperm whale families share patterns of clicks called codas. Teams of scientists are recording thousands of them, and nobody can yet say what they mean.
Humans have many scent glands, but no human pheromone has been purified and shown to work in careful tests.

open_questions.q: How much do plants signal to each other?
open_questions.why_open: Plants give off chemicals when they are eaten, and neighbours respond. Scientists argue about how much of this is signalling and how common it is.

open_questions.q: What is echolocation like for a bat?
open_questions.why_open: We can measure a bat's calls and her brain. We have no way yet to find out how her echoes feel to her. They may feel like hearing, like seeing, or like something we have no word for.

maths.problem: In the Smell Mark Test, one square out of four carries the mark. Suppose you had no sense of smell and guessed all 8 times. About how many would you get right? If you got 7 right, was it luck?
maths.answer: About 2 right by guessing. Getting 7 right is very unlikely to be luck.
maths.explain: One square in four is marked, so a guess is right about 1 time in 4. 8 divided by 4 is 2. A score of 7 is far above 2, so the nose was doing the work.
maths.context: In the Smell Mark Test you sniff four paper squares with your eyes covered. You say which one carries the smell mark.
maths.why_maths: Knowing what guessing alone would give tells you whether your result means anything.

maths.problem: Here are four scores out of 10 from the Echo Plate Test. At 10 centimetres the score was 9. At 30 centimetres it was 7. At 60 centimetres it was 5. In silence it was 5. Guessing gives about 5. At which distances did the echo clearly help?
maths.explain: 9 and 7 are both above 5, and 9 is far above it. The scores of 5 are what guessing gives. So at 60 centimetres and in silence there is no sign that the echo helped.
maths.context: In the Echo Plate Test you say 'shhh' with your eyes covered. You tell whether a steel plate is in front of your face. These are made-up scores.
maths.why_maths: Comparing each score with the guessing score shows where the echo really carried information.

maths.problem: Sound travels about 34 centimetres in one thousandth of a second. A bat hears the echo from a moth 10 thousandths of a second after her call. How far away is the moth?
maths.explain: In 10 thousandths of a second, sound travels 10 times 34, which is 340 centimetres. The sound went to the moth and back, so the moth is half of that distance away. Half of 340 is 170.
maths.context: In the Echo Plate Test you found a plate by its echo. A bat does the same, and she also times the echo.
maths.why_maths: The echo makes a round trip, so the time must be turned into a distance and then halved. This is how a bat's brain and a ship's sonar measure distance.

maths.problem: In one tenth of a second, sound travels 34 metres in air and 150 metres in water. A bat and a dolphin each hear an echo one tenth of a second after calling. How far away is each one's target?
maths.answer: The bat's target is 17 metres away. The dolphin's target is 75 metres away.
maths.explain: The sound goes there and back, so halve each distance. Half of 34 is 17. Half of 150 is 75. Sound is faster in water, so the same wait means a target more than four times as far.
maths.context: Bats in air and dolphins in water both find things by timing echoes. Sound travels faster in water than in air.
maths.why_maths: Halving the round trip for two speeds shows why a dolphin's echoes reach further than a bat's in the same time.

maths.problem: In Signal Spotting, a watcher counted 20 signals: 9 sound, 7 sight, 3 touch and 1 smell. What fraction were sound or sight? A dog watched the same street. Would the dog's fractions be the same?
maths.answer: 16 out of 20, which is four fifths. The dog's fractions would probably be very different, with far more smell.
maths.explain: 9 plus 7 is 16. 16 out of 20 is the same as 4 out of 5. The count shows what a human can notice. A dog's nose picks up many smell signals that we miss.
maths.context: In Signal Spotting you watch a street for five minutes and count the signals on each channel. These are made-up counts.
maths.why_maths: A fraction shows which channels fill a watcher's count. It also makes clear that the count depends on who is counting.

maths.problem: A child rates the strength of a vinegar mark from 0 to 5. The ratings are 5 at 0 minutes, 4 at 10 minutes, 2 at 30 minutes and 0 at 60 minutes. Did the smell fade by the same amount every 10 minutes? When did it fade fastest?
maths.answer: No. It fell fastest in the first 30 minutes, by about 1 point every 10 minutes, and more slowly after that.
maths.explain: From 0 to 10 minutes it fell by 1. From 10 to 30 minutes it fell by 2, which is 1 for each 10 minutes. From 30 to 60 minutes it fell by 2, which is less than 1 for each 10 minutes.
maths.context: In the Smell Mark Test you sniff a vinegar mark at 0, 10, 30 and 60 minutes. These are made-up strength ratings for that mark.
maths.why_maths: Looking at the size of each drop, not only the last number, shows how a smell signal fades over time.

how_we_found_out.story: For a long time people thought a male moth found a female by seeing her or hearing her. More than a hundred years ago, in the south of France, the insect watcher Jean-Henri Fabre tested this. A female great peacock moth came out of her cocoon in his study. He put her under a wire cover. That night dozens of large male moths flew in through the window. Fabre then tried a female under a glass cover, where males could see her. He wrote that they ignored her, and went to the place where she had rested before. So sight was not what brought them. Something that passed through wire, but not through glass, was drawing them. Fabre could not say what. The answer came in 1959. The German chemist Adolf Butenandt and his team had worked on the problem for about twenty years. They used the scent glands of around 500,000 female silk moths. They purified one chemical and named it bombykol. A trace of bombykol alone made male silk moths flutter and walk towards it. In the same year Peter Karlson and Martin Lüscher gave such chemicals the name pheromones.
how_we_found_out.who: Jean-Henri Fabre in France, then Adolf Butenandt and his team in Germany, and Peter Karlson and Martin Lüscher, who made the word pheromone
how_we_found_out.when: Fabre published his moth tests in 1900. Butenandt's team named bombykol in 1959, and the word pheromone was made in the same year.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That a male moth finds a female by seeing or hearing her. Fabre showed that males ignored a female they could see under glass. Butenandt's team then showed that one chemical from her body is enough to draw the males.
how_we_found_out.art: An old study at night with an open window, a wire cover on a table with a large moth under it, and many moths flying in around a lamp.

roots.context: In this unit you left smell marks on paper and found a steel plate by its echo. Here we ask what a message is, and whether a message needs its sender to be there.

deep_truth.truth: In the Smell Mark Test, your nose found the clove mark long after the sender had left the room. A call or a wave ends when the sender stops. A smell mark goes on giving its message while the sender is far away. So one tigress can warn others off many trees at once, without being at any of them.
deep_truth.habit: We think of a message as something that passes between two beings who are together, as when we talk. A scent mark needs no meeting. The sender and the receiver may never see each other.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Smell Mark Test the grown-up who made the marks stayed away. The clove mark was usually still found after 60 minutes. Tigers, dogs and cats leave marks that others read hours or days later. Fabre wrote that male moths went to the place where a female had rested, after she had been moved.

three.who_am_i: You send signals all day on all four channels, and you chose only some of them. You are also an animal who writes. Writing is a mark that works while you are away.
three.what_is_life: No living being lives without sending and receiving. Even bacteria give off chemicals that other bacteria sense and act on.
three.what_is_this_world: The air, the water and the ground are full of messages. Most were not meant for us, and many are beyond our senses.

roots.thread: A signal is never the work of one being. A moth's pheromone does nothing without an antenna built to catch it. A peacock's train does nothing without a peahen's eye. Over millions of years, senders and receivers have shaped each other's bodies. Many sages taught that all beings are one life in many bodies. The science here says something close. All animals share ancestors, and that is partly why a dog's growl makes sense to you.

teachings.teaching: The hymn says that speech is measured out in four parts. Three parts are kept hidden, and humans speak only the fourth.
teachings.link: The hymn is about sacred speech, and it is not about animals. Yet its picture fits what this unit found. The talk that humans can hear is a small part of all the signalling around us. Bat calls, elephant rumbles and pheromones were hidden from us until instruments found them.

teachings.teaching: Zhuangzi and his friend Huizi stand on a bridge over the Hao river. Zhuangzi says the fish are enjoying themselves. Huizi asks: you are not a fish, so how do you know what fish enjoy?
teachings.link: Scientists meet Huizi's question with every signal. They cannot ask a frog what his foot wave means. They can only test what other frogs do when they see it.

science.text: Even bacteria signal. Many kinds give off chemicals and sense how much has built up around them. When there are enough of them, they act together. This is called quorum sensing.
In 1974 the philosopher Thomas Nagel asked what it is like to be a bat. He argued that we could learn everything about echolocation and still not know how it feels to the bat.

other_view.who: Many biologists, following a rule that C. Lloyd Morgan set out in 1894
other_view.view: A tigress who sprays a tree may not intend to tell anyone anything. Marking may be an urge passed down from her ancestors, because tigers who marked their land had fewer fights. On this view we should not say she 'sends a message' unless simpler explanations fail.

playtest: Read through as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, step by step, but not yet done at home. The Smell Mark Test (core) needs 8 paper squares, vinegar or lemon juice, one clove, a spoon and two plates. It takes about 30 minutes of doing, spread over one hour of waiting. Start it early in the session and use the waits for the cards or the story. The expected result is that the vinegar mark is hard to find after 30 to 60 minutes and the clove mark lasts until the next day. A fan, an open window or a very humid day changes the timing, and lemon juice may fade more slowly than vinegar. So the steps say to record what really happens. The Echo Plate Test (core) needs a large steel plate, a cloth and a quiet room. Most people hear the 'shhh' change with the plate at 10 centimetres, fewer at 30 centimetres, and at 60 centimetres the score is usually close to guessing. The silent round checks for other clues such as warm air. Switch off a noisy fan if you can. Three Strings works with any thin string or wool pulled tight. The Waving Test needs a dim room. In a small bright flat every signal may be easy to read, so the step says to dim the room or stand further apart. Nestmate or Stranger needs a grown-up to make the packets, and four kitchen smells that differ clearly. Message Through the Noise needs about five big steps of clear floor. No part needs a garden, a pet or a wild animal. Signal Spotting works at any window, or indoors with the family. Facts to treat with care: Fabre's account is from his own book of 1900, and the year of his moth night is not given here. The numbers for bombykol (about twenty years, around 500,000 moths) are the usual rounded figures. Elephant rumbles reaching 'several kilometres' depends on the weather. The fading time of an ant alarm pheromone, about a minute, comes from work on harvester ants. Whether peahens choose by eyespots is marked as debated. The Rig Veda verse is given as a paraphrase, and the unit says plainly that the verse is not about animals. The three videos have no address yet.
